module.title: Overpopulation vs Overconsumption
module.summary: Whether environmental damage is driven by population or consumption: carrying capacity, Malthus, IPAT, technology's dual role, overconsumption and the ecological footprint.

nodes.label: Week 3: Overpopulation vs Overconsumption
nodes.summary: Is environmental damage driven by how many people there are, or by how much and how they consume?
nodes.details:
Week 3 asks whether the planet's limits are threatened mainly by **population** or by **consumption**. It is organised in four parts:

- **3.1 Planetary boundaries & carrying capacity** - carrying capacity, J vs S growth curves, **Malthus** and **Neo-Malthusian** views, overpopulation, technology and the demographic transition, and the **Kerala** case.
- **3.2 Thinking about environmental impact** - the **IPAT** equation (Ehrlich & Holdren), P and A data, the 2050 'factor five' scenario, the **dual role of technology**, the **Jevons paradox**, Kuznets/Kurzweil optimism and **environmental justice** (offshoring, EV batteries, AI data centres).
- **3.3 Over-consumption** - overconsumption, addictive consumption and **hyperconsumption**.
- **3.4 Ecological footprint** - footprint vs **biocapacity**, measurement in global hectares, Indonesia's deficit and 'how many Earths'.

The through-line: **population size alone does not determine impact** - affluence, technology, distribution and governance matter, and the richest consume far more than their share.

nodes.label: Part 3.1: Planetary Limits & Carrying Capacity
nodes.summary: Earth has limits; population growth, technology and development interact with carrying capacity.
nodes.details:
Part 3.1 links last week's **planetary boundaries** to the ecological idea of **carrying capacity** and then to the historical population debate.

- Starts from the 'take-home message' of Rio+20: development must stay within planetary limits.
- **Carrying capacity**: limiting factors cap population growth (S-shaped curve).
- **Malthus** (resources grow linearly, population exponentially -> crisis) and the **Neo-Malthusians** (social, economic and technological drivers of scarcity; Barry Commoner on technology).
- World population data (1 billion in 1804 -> 8 billion in 2022) and the distinction between **population growth** and **overpopulation**.
- Technology (Green Revolution) raises *effective* carrying capacity; GDP-energy-emission data show the link is not proportional.
- **Demographic transition**: falling population may be an *effect* of development rather than its cause, illustrated by **Kerala, India**.

nodes.label: Future We Want & Safe Operating Space
nodes.summary: Since Rio 1992 development must balance economy, society and environment within planetary boundaries; 7 of 9 already breached.
nodes.details:
The opening 'take-home message' frames the week, citing **'The Future We Want' (Rio+20, 2012)** and **'Realizing the Future We Want for All' (2019)**.

- Since the **Rio Earth Summit (1992)** the world has agreed to steer development by the **compass of sustainability**: economic progress in harmony with **social justice** and **environmental preservation** (the three pillars).
- Human activity must stay within the **planetary boundaries**, the **safe operating space** for humanity (Rockstrom et al.).
- Recall from the previous lecture: **7 out of 9 planetary boundaries have been breached**.

Why it matters: carrying capacity, the ecological footprint and overshoot (later in this week) are all ways of asking whether humanity is living within these limits. It connects Week 2 (planetary boundaries) to Week 3's question of *who* and *what* pushes us past them.

nodes.label: Carrying Capacity
nodes.summary: Maximum number of individuals of a species a habitat can sustainably support, set by limiting factors; growth follows an S-curve.
nodes.details:
**Carrying capacity (K)** is the **maximum number of individuals of a species that a particular habitat can sustainably support**.

- It is set by **limiting factors**: **space**, **abiotic** factors (water, nutrients, climate) and **biotic** factors (e.g. **disease**, predators, competition).
- **J-curve (exponential growth)**: happens when resources are effectively unlimited, i.e. early on, when the population is still far below K.
- **S-curve (logistic growth)**: as the population approaches K, growth slows and levels off. In reality there is **no unlimited population growth** - every population eventually meets limits (lecture notes, after Spoolman & Miller 2019).

For humans the idea is tricky because **technology and trade raise the *effective* carrying capacity** (see agricultural technology), and because impact depends on consumption, not just numbers. **Overpopulation** is defined *relative* to carrying capacity, and the **ecological footprint vs biocapacity** comparison is the modern accounting version of the same idea.
nodes.examTips: Define carrying capacity and name the three groups of limiting factors. Explain J vs S curve. Link to overpopulation (needs exceed carrying capacity) and to footprint vs biocapacity.

nodes.label: Malthus, Neo-Malthus & Overpopulation
nodes.summary: The classic debate on whether population growth outruns resources, and when growth becomes 'overpopulation'.
nodes.details:
This cluster covers the intellectual history of the population-resources debate:

- **Thomas Robert Malthus** - population grows **geometrically**, food/resources **arithmetically**, so crisis (famine, disease, war) eventually pulls population back down.
- **World population data (1700-2022)** - exponential growth in recent centuries raises the question of whether Malthus was right.
- **Overpopulation** - not the same as population growth: it occurs when the population's needs **sustainably exceed carrying capacity**, shaped also by consumption, technology, distribution and governance (Paul Ehrlich, *The Population Bomb*).
- **Neo-Malthusian theory** - widens Malthus to social, economic and environmental interactions; **Barry Commoner** argued **technology** matters more than numbers.

These positions set up Part 3.2's **IPAT** equation, which combines population, affluence and technology in one formula.

nodes.label: Malthusian View
nodes.summary: Malthus: resources grow arithmetically, population geometrically, so crises (famine, disease, war) push population back to sustainable levels.
nodes.details:
**Thomas Robert Malthus** (*Essay on the Principle of Population*, 1798) lived through rapid population growth in England.

- **Natural resources (food) have fixed limits and grow arithmetically/linearly** (1, 2, 3, 4...).
- **Population tends to grow exponentially/geometrically** (1, 2, 4, 8...).
- The gap eventually produces a **crisis period** - **famine, epidemics and war** - that reduces population back to what the environment can sustain.

Lecturer's notes: Malthus diagnosed an **imbalance between a habitat's resources and population size**. His work is now seen as the **first systematic study of ecological limits to growth in a finite world** and an early source of sustainability thinking, but in his day it got little attention because national or global environmental issues were not yet part of political or social discourse.

**Critique / limits**: the chart says nothing about changes in resource *use*; Malthus underestimated **technology** (Green Revolution raised food output) and the **demographic transition** (fertility falls with development).
nodes.examTips: Classic question: explain Malthus's argument and why his prediction has not (yet) fully materialised (technology, demographic transition). Compare with Neo-Malthusians and with IPAT.

nodes.label: World Population Growth Data
nodes.details:
The slide (UN DESA, *World Population Prospects 2022*) shows **exponential growth** of the human population from 1700 to 2022, with projections to 2100.

**Billion milestones:**
- 1 bn - **1804**
- 2 bn - **1927** (123 years later)
- 3 bn - **1960**; 4 bn - **1974**; 5 bn - **1987**; 6 bn - **1998**; 7 bn - **2010**
- 8 bn - **2022**; projected 9 bn - **2037**; 10 bn - **2058** (median projection, with a widening 95% prediction interval)

Each extra billion now arrives in ~12-13 years, but the projection curve **flattens** later in the century, consistent with the **demographic transition**.

Discussion questions on the slide: Is this in line with **Malthus's** claim of a population-resource imbalance? What is the relationship between humans and the environment? Can resource shortages be avoided, and do we have the ability to overcome them? A related chart (s18, US Census Bureau 2010) shows 3 bn in ~1960 rising toward ~9 bn by ~2045.

nodes.label: Overpopulation
nodes.summary: Occurs when population needs sustainably exceed the system's carrying capacity; depends on consumption, technology, distribution and governance, not size alone.
nodes.details:
The lecture separates three ideas:

1. **Population growth** - the number of people increases over time; rates **vary across regions**. It is a *demographic fact*.
2. **Population pressure** - demand for **food, water, energy, land, housing and infrastructure** rises as population grows.
3. **Overpopulation** - occurs **when the needs of the population sustainably exceed the carrying capacity** of the system.

Key point: overpopulation is **not determined by population size alone**. It is also shaped by **consumption levels, technology, resource distribution and governance**. Two regions with the same population do not necessarily face the same pressure.

The concept traces to **Paul Ehrlich, *The Population Bomb* (1968)**. Lecturer's summary: *population growth is a demographic fact; overpopulation is about the relationship between population and the capacity of the system to support it*. This anticipates **IPAT** (Ehrlich & Holdren) and the **overconsumption** argument: India's huge population lives within <1 Earth while the USA needs ~5.
nodes.examTips: Common confusion: population growth does not equal overpopulation. Be ready to explain why the same population can be 'overpopulated' in one place and not another (consumption, technology, distribution, governance).

nodes.label: Neo-Malthusian Theory & Technology
nodes.summary: Extends Malthus to social, economic and environmental interactions causing scarcity; Barry Commoner stressed technology over population numbers.
nodes.details:
**Neo-Malthusian theory** updates Malthus for modern environmental problems.

- It **recognises interactions of social, economic and environmental factors** that lead to environmental damage and **natural-resource scarcity**, but keeps the core premise: **resources are becoming scarcer and environmental damage is occurring**.
- The slide graph: a red **population** curve rising exponentially, a green **food production** line rising linearly; where they cross is a **crisis point (war, famine, etc.)**.
- Neo-Malthusians propose **population control** plus **more efficient resource use**. The theory gained attention in the late 19th and 20th centuries amid overpopulation concerns.

**Role of technology - Barry Commoner** (*The Closing Circle*, 1971): **technology has a greater environmental impact than population numbers**. Post-war technologies such as **petrochemical-based economies, pesticides and fossil fuels** sharply increased environmental impact.

This sets up the **Ehrlich-Commoner debate** that IPAT resolves: impact depends on P **and** A **and** T. It also foreshadows the **dual role of technology**.
nodes.examTips: Contrast Malthus (food vs population only) with Neo-Malthusians (social-economic-environmental interactions) and with Commoner (technology > population).

nodes.label: Technology, Development & Population
nodes.summary: Technology raises effective carrying capacity; development lowers birth rates; wealth does not map neatly to impact or wellbeing.
nodes.details:
This cluster asks whether the Malthusian trap is inevitable.

- **GDP, energy and CO2 data** - bigger economies use more energy and emit more, but **not proportionally**; efficiency and energy mix matter.
- **Agricultural technology** - extensification -> intensification -> **Green Revolution**; raises the *effective* carrying capacity, with trade-offs.
- **Demographic transition** - population decline may be an **effect** of economic development, not its cause.
- **Kerala case** - high human development without high income.

Together they show that **population is not destiny**: technology, development, health and education reshape the population-environment relationship, which is why Part 3.2 moves to IPAT.

nodes.label: GDP, Energy & CO2 Emissions Data
nodes.summary: Larger/richer economies use more energy and emit more, but not proportionally: efficiency and energy sources matter (2021 country data).
nodes.details:
Two 2021 tables compare the top-10 economies.

**Totals (s10)**: bigger economies generally use more energy and emit more, **but not proportionally**.
- **USA**: GDP rank 1 (~US$23.3 trillion), energy 93.4 EJ (rank 2), CO2 ~5,007 Mt (rank 2).
- **China**: GDP rank 2 (~$17.8 tn) but **rank 1 in energy (157.9 EJ) and CO2 (~11,472 Mt)**.
- **India**: GDP rank 5 but rank 3 in energy and CO2 (~2,710 Mt).
- **UK, France, Italy**: high GDP with relatively low emissions (~306-347 Mt).

**Per capita (s11)**: higher GDP per capita tends to mean higher energy use, but **emissions also depend on efficiency and energy source**.
- USA $70,219 -> 14.86 t CO2/person; Canada 14.30 t; South Korea 11.89 t.
- France $43,659 -> only **4.74 t** (nuclear-heavy mix); UK 5.15 t.
- India $2,238 -> **1.93 t**; China $12,618 -> 8.05 t.

Lesson: population and GDP alone don't predict impact - this motivates **IPAT** (affluence *and* technology).

nodes.label: Agricultural Technology & Green Revolution
nodes.summary: Agricultural innovation (extensification to intensification, Green Revolution) raised effective carrying capacity; shifted goal from food sufficiency to food security, with trade-offs.
nodes.details:
Humans **do not rely solely on natural productivity**: **agricultural innovation** lets us meet food needs and so **increases the effective carrying capacity** for human populations - a key reason Malthus's prediction did not come true.

- **Extensification** = opening new land; **intensification** = higher yields on the same land through improved seeds, fertiliser, irrigation, pesticides, mechanisation and better markets.
- The peak was the **Green Revolution**, which boosted productivity and reduced hunger in many countries.
- Policy goal shifted from **food sufficiency** (how much is produced) to **food security**, with four pillars: **availability, access** (purchasing power/distribution), **utilisation** (nutrition/safety) and **stability** over time.

**Trade-offs of intensification**: soil and water degradation/**pollution**, **GHG emissions**, **loss of biodiversity**. Hence the next step is **sustainable/regenerative intensification**, keeping productivity while shrinking the footprint and building resilience to economic and climate shocks.

An early example of the **dual role of technology** (Part 3.2).

nodes.label: Demographic Transition: Limit as Effect
nodes.summary: Population decline is an effect, not a cause, of development: as poverty falls, death then birth rates drop and growth stabilises.
nodes.details:
Slide title: **'Limit to population: an effect rather than the cause?'** Will population grow without limit once technology raises food supply? Not necessarily: social change, health and education also shape it.

**Demographic transition model** (lecturer's notes):
1. **Low/no growth** - high birth *and* death rates (poor health care, sanitation, food).
2. **Falling death rate** - public health improves, births stay high -> **rapid growth** (typical of developing countries).
3. **Falling birth rate** - driven by **economic development / poverty reduction** and financial success that gives access to **education, health care and birth control**; growth slows.
4. **Low/no growth** - low birth and death rates; population near equilibrium (developed countries).

Key message: **economic development -> poverty reduction -> population decline**, i.e. falling population is **a result of successful development, not its precondition**. The slide also floats the alternative framing: financial success as a 'prerequisite' for human development - which the **Kerala** case challenges.
nodes.examTips: Explain the four stages and why lower fertility is an outcome of development. Use Kerala as a counter-example showing human development without high income.

nodes.label: Case Study: Kerala, India
nodes.summary: Kerala has low per-capita income (~US$3,100) yet literacy (94%) and life expectancy (75) comparable to developed countries.
nodes.details:
**Kerala, India** shows that **high human development does not require high income**.

2022 data (World Population Data; Our World in Data):

| | Kerala | India | Australia | Germany | USA | Indonesia |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Population (m) | 36 | 1,380 | 25.5 | 83.8 | 341 | 275 |
| GDP per capita (US$) | 3,100 | 2,375 | 63,945 | 48,429 | 58,487 | 3,895 |
| Density (/km2) | 860 | 488 | 3.5 | 242 | 37.8 | 141 |
| Literacy (%) | 94 | 69.4 | ~100 | ~100 | ~100 | 94 |
| Life expectancy (yr) | 75 | 67.3 | 83.1 | 80.5 | 77.5 | 68.3 |

- Kerala's income is below Indonesia's, and it is **very densely populated (860/km2)**, yet its **literacy (94%)** and **life expectancy (75)** approach rich-country levels and beat India's average.
- Lecturer's conclusion: **high economic capacity does not automatically raise human development** - investment in education and health does.

Links: supports the demographic transition argument (education/health lower fertility) and challenges the idea that GDP growth is the only route to wellbeing.
nodes.examTips: Know the headline numbers (GDP ~$3,100; literacy 94%; life expectancy 75; density 860/km2) and the lesson: human development is not just a function of income.

nodes.label: Part 3.2: Thinking About Environmental Impact
nodes.summary: From population to impact: IPAT, technology's dual role, Jevons paradox, Kuznets optimism and unequal/unjust distribution of impacts.
nodes.details:
Part 3.2 moves from population numbers to **environmental impact**.

- Population size affects **total demand**, but populous countries don't always have the highest per-capita energy use or emissions. Impact also depends on **consumption levels** and **how needs are produced (technology)**.
- **IPAT** (Ehrlich & Holdren 1974): I = P x A x T, with P/A data and a **2050 scenario** requiring technology to cut impact by a **factor of five**.
- **Dual role of technology**: it can improve or worsen impact; **technofix** optimism; the **Jevons paradox** (rebound/backfire).
- **Kuznets & Kurzweil**: does rising affluence eventually reduce impact?
- **Environmental justice**: impacts are borne by those who don't enjoy the benefits - offshoring, EV battery minerals, AI data centres.

nodes.label: IPAT Equation
nodes.summary: I = P x A x T: impact equals Population x Affluence (consumption/income per capita) x Technology (impact per unit); Ehrlich & Holdren 1974.
nodes.details:
**IPAT**, from **Ehrlich & Holdren (1974)**, says that environmental damage comes not only from population but also from consumption:

**I = P x A x T**
- **I - Impact** on the environment (e.g. emissions, resource use).
- **P - Population** (number of people).
- **A - Affluence**, measured as the **level of consumption per person** or **per-capita income**.
- **T - Technology**, the impact per unit of consumption (how goods and energy are produced).

**Why it matters**
- It moves beyond the pure Malthusian focus on numbers: a large population with low consumption (India) can have less impact than a smaller, richer one (USA).
- It reconciles **Ehrlich** (population) with **Commoner** (technology): all three factors multiply.
- It frames policy: since P and A are rising, **T must fall** (decoupling) to keep I constant - see the 2050 scenario.

**Limits**: the factors are not independent (technology can raise consumption, see **Jevons paradox**), and the equation ignores distribution and justice.
nodes.examTips: Most likely exam item. State the formula, define each term (A = consumption/income per capita), name the authors (Ehrlich & Holdren 1974), and explain why T can raise or lower I. Do a simple calculation (e.g. P x1.35, A x4 -> T must fall ~5x).

nodes.label: P and A Data: Population & GDP Trends
nodes.summary: Charts of world population (3 bn 1960 to ~9 bn 2045) and world real GDP growth (1999-2010) illustrate rising P and A.
nodes.details:
Slide 18 shows the two growing IPAT drivers (source: *Sustainability: A Comprehensive Foundation*, IPAT chapter):

- **P - World Population 1950-2050** (US Census Bureau, International Data Base, Dec 2010): **3 billion ~1960, 4 bn ~1974, 5 bn ~1987, 6 bn ~1999, 7 bn ~2012, 8 bn ~2026, 9 bn ~2045** - steady near-linear growth of ~1 billion every 12-14 years.
- **A - Worldwide growth of real GDP 1999-2010** (CIA World Factbook via IndexMundi): annual world real growth mostly **~3-5%** (e.g. ~4.8% in 2000, ~5.2% in 2006-07), a dip to **~-0.7% in 2009** (global financial crisis), and a rebound to **~4.9% in 2010**.

Takeaway: both **population and affluence keep rising**, so unless **T (technology)** improves dramatically, **impact I** will grow. This is the basis for the 2050 'factor five' calculation.

nodes.label: 2050 Scenario: Factor-Five Decoupling
nodes.summary: To keep 2050 environmental quality at 2010 levels with population +35% and affluence about x4, technology impact must fall by a factor of ~5.
nodes.details:
Applying IPAT: **how can environmental quality in 2050 be kept as it is now?**

Assumptions (base year 2010):
- **Population rises ~35%** by 2050 -> P x 1.35.
- **Affluence rises about 4 times** -> A x 4.
- If technology stayed constant, **I = 1.35 x 4 = 5.4 times** today's impact.

To keep **I constant**, technology must **'decouple'** - cut impact per unit of consumption **by a factor of about five** (T reduced to ~1/5 of 2010 levels).

Why it matters:
- Shows how IPAT turns into a **quantitative policy target** (the 'Factor Five' idea of resource productivity).
- Shows the burden falls on **technology and consumption patterns**, since population and income growth are hard to stop.
- Raises the question of whether technology can deliver this without **rebound effects** (Jevons paradox) - setting up the dual-role and over-consumption discussions.
nodes.examTips: Be able to reproduce the arithmetic: 1.35 x 4 = 5.4, so T must fall ~5x. Explain what 'decoupling' means.

nodes.label: Dual Role of Technology
nodes.summary: Technology can reduce impact (efficiency, renewables, monitoring, innovation) or increase it (more exploitation, pollution, waste, consumption).
nodes.details:
If technology advances, can it solve environmental problems? The **technofix** view (attributed on the slide to Kurzweil) says yes. The lecture instead stresses technology's **dual role**:

**Improving environmental impact**
- **Efficiency** in using and managing natural resources
- **Renewable energy**
- **Pollution monitoring**
- **Innovation**

**Worsening environmental impact**
- **Expansion of natural-resource exploitation**
- **Pollution and waste**
- **Increasing consumption**

Examples (s20): **coal power plants** generally **increase GHG emissions**, while **solar power reduces** them. Yet coal can **reduce deforestation** if it replaces **firewood** as a cheap energy source - the same technology can be harmful in one respect and helpful in another.

Connections: T in **IPAT** can push I up or down; the **Jevons paradox** shows efficiency gains can backfire; **Barry Commoner** emphasised the harmful side; **environmental justice** cases (EV batteries, AI) show 'green' technology shifting burdens elsewhere.
nodes.examTips: Give two examples each of technology improving and worsening impact. Explain the coal-vs-firewood nuance. Link to IPAT's T and to Jevons paradox.

nodes.label: Jevons Paradox: Rebound & Backfire
nodes.summary: Efficiency gains can raise total resource use: rebound (consumption offsets savings) and backfire (overconsumption exceeds savings).
nodes.details:
**Jevons Paradox**: technological progress makes resource use **more efficient**, but it has also **increased total consumption** of natural resources. (Named after William Stanley Jevons, who observed in 1865 that more efficient steam engines increased Britain's coal use.)

The slide distinguishes:
- **Rebound** - increased consumption eats into the efficiency savings (the slide labels this RE = 1).
- **Backfire** - consumption rises so much (**overconsumption**) that total use exceeds what it was before the efficiency gain (slide label RE < 1).

*Note:* the RE notation follows the slide; many textbooks instead describe backfire as a rebound effect **greater than 100%**. Know the concepts: rebound = savings partly/fully offset; backfire = efficiency leads to *more* total use.

Why cheaper/efficient = more use: lower cost per unit makes the good more attractive, so people use more of it (e.g. fuel-efficient cars driven further, LED lights left on).

Connects the **T** and **A** terms of IPAT (they are not independent) and bridges to **over-consumption** in Part 3.3.
nodes.examTips: Classic trick question: 'Does efficiency always reduce resource use?' Answer with Jevons paradox; distinguish rebound vs backfire.

nodes.label: Kuznets & Kurzweil: Affluence Reduces Impact?
nodes.summary: Claim: rising affluence plus advanced technology eventually lowers impact (e.g. reforestation in W. Europe/US vs loss in Brazil/Indonesia). Is it true?
nodes.details:
**Claim (Kuznets and Kurzweil)**: as **affluence** rises and technology advances, **environmental impact declines**. This echoes the **Environmental Kuznets Curve** - impact rises in early development, then falls after a certain income level - plus Kurzweil-style techno-optimism.

**Evidence offered**: **reforestation** has increased in **Western Europe and the US**, while forests have **decreased in Brazil and Indonesia**.

**Question posed: is the argument true?** Model answer outline:
- *Partly*: richer countries can afford cleaner technology, stronger regulation and conservation; some local indicators (forests, air quality) improve.
- *But*: rich countries often **outsource** land-use and pollution through trade - forests regrow at home while imports drive deforestation in Brazil/Indonesia (see **unequal impact / offshoring**).
- **Consumption-based** CO2 and **ecological footprints** of rich countries remain highest (USA ~5 Earths).
- **Global** impacts (GHG, biodiversity) don't follow the curve neatly; rebound effects can offset gains.

Conclusion: affluence can improve *local* indicators but often **displaces** impacts rather than eliminating them.
nodes.examTips: Be ready to critique: displacement via trade/offshoring, consumption-based accounting, footprint data.

nodes.label: Unequal Impact & Environmental Justice
nodes.summary: Environmental impacts are often borne by those who do not enjoy the benefits: producing countries, local communities, low- and middle-income countries.
nodes.details:
**Unequal environmental impact**: impacts are **not always borne by those who enjoy the benefits**. Goods consumed in one country can **use resources** in another and **generate emissions and pollution in the producing country**, while the benefits are enjoyed in the importing country.

Examples (s24):
- **Smartphones** - used in consumer countries, minerals mined elsewhere.
- **Fast fashion** - clothes consumed in one country; **water, energy and production waste** occur in the producing region.
- **Agricultural commodities** - consumption in importing countries linked to **land-use change** in producing countries.

**Environmental justice** asks who bears these burdens. Mechanisms and cases:
- **Offshoring** of polluting production to LMICs.
- **EV battery minerals** - 'green' transport with extraction impacts in Chile and the DR Congo.
- **AI data centres** - global benefits, local energy and water burdens.
- The **EJAtlas** (ejatlas.org, Martinez-Alier 2023) maps thousands of environmental conflicts worldwide - largest categories include **mineral ores/building materials, fossil fuels & climate justice, and biomass/land conflicts**.

This is the bridge to Week 4's **Global North vs Global South**.
nodes.examTips: Explain with an example why consumption in one country causes impacts in another. Link to Global North/South and consumption-based emissions.

nodes.label: Offshoring & Environmental Externalities
nodes.summary: Transnational firms relocate production and source raw materials in LMICs with looser regulation, shifting environmental damage onto others.
nodes.details:
**Offshoring** is the practice of **transnational corporations relocating production facilities** and **sourcing raw materials from low- and middle-income countries (LMICs)**, which often have **looser environmental regulations**.

- **Since the 1970s**, many **North American and European companies** moved production to **Latin America and Asia**.
- Result: **environmental externalities** - environmental damage **borne by other parties** than those who profit or consume (Robbins et al., 2014, *Environment & Society*).
- The **EJAtlas** map of environmental conflicts (Martinez-Alier, 2023) shows dense clusters of conflicts in Latin America, Africa, South and Southeast Asia, consistent with impacts being exported.

Why it matters:
- It explains how rich countries can show falling domestic pollution or rising forest cover (the **Kuznets** claim) while their **consumption-based** impact stays high.
- It is a core argument for **consumption-based accounting** (CO2 per capita by consumption, ecological footprint) rather than production-based national inventories.

nodes.label: Case: EV Batteries (LFP vs NMC)
nodes.summary: EVs cut emissions but drive mineral demand (cobalt x39.6 by 2030); LFP batteries have far lower GWP and water use than NMC.
nodes.details:
**Electric vehicles** show technology's dual role and environmental justice together.

**Benefits**: in **China**, EV policies can contribute significantly to **climate mitigation, air-quality improvement and public health** (Hsieh et al., 2022).

**Mineral demand**: by **2030** (vs 2015) demand for **cobalt x39.6, lithium x19.6, manganese x5.2, nickel x4.7** (Jones et al., 2020), much of it from **developing regions**.

**Extraction impacts** (Prates et al., 2023): **groundwater depletion from lithium mining in Chile**; **unsafe working conditions and child labour** in **DR Congo** cobalt mines.

**Two battery chemistries**:
- **LFP** - lithium-iron-phosphate; **NMC** - nickel-manganese-cobalt (higher energy density, longer range).
- **GWP of production: NMC ~1,208 vs LFP ~573 kg CO2-eq**; **water use: NMC ~153.6 vs LFP ~25.8** (per unit, per the LCA cited).
- LFP also performs better on several air/water pollution and toxicity indicators.
- Industry response: **~70% of EVs in China use LFP**.

**'How about Indonesia?'** - the government promotes **nickel-based** batteries (Indonesia's large nickel reserves) while makers such as BYD still rely on LFP: a live trade-off between industrial policy and footprint.
nodes.examTips: Know that LFP has roughly half the GWP and ~1/6 the water use of NMC, and why Indonesia's nickel strategy is relevant.

nodes.label: Case: AI Data Centres' Energy Demand
nodes.summary: Data centres used ~415 TWh (1.5% of global electricity) in 2024, projected ~945 TWh by 2030 driven by AI; impacts concentrate locally.
nodes.details:
**AI requires data centres that demand large amounts of electricity** (IEA, *Energy and AI*).

- **2024**: data centres consumed **~415 TWh**, about **1.5% of global electricity consumption**.
- **2030 projection**: **~945 TWh** (more than double), with **AI as the primary driver**.
- The IEA map (slide 28) shows data centres are **clustered** - largest clusters named include **Northern Virginia, Chicago, Dallas, Omaha** (US), **Dublin, London** (Europe), **Beijing, Shanghai, Pearl River Delta, Singapore** (Asia) - **potentially creating challenges for local electricity systems**.

**Justice question** on the slide: while **AI's benefits are enjoyed by many**, its **energy and water demands are concentrated where data centres are built** - are these impacts distributed equitably?

Connections: another example of technology's **dual role** (digital efficiency vs new energy demand), a possible **Jevons**-type rebound, and of **unequal impact** between beneficiaries and host communities.

nodes.label: Part 3.3: Over-Consumption
nodes.summary: Consumption beyond need or beyond ecosystem recovery drives damage; includes addictive consumption and hyperconsumption, concentrated among the richest.
nodes.details:
Part 3.3 shifts the blame question from population to **consumption**.

- **Overconsumption**: consumption so excessive it **drives environmental damage**; consumption behaviour can be rational, cultural, pleasurable, identity-based or communicative.
- **Evidence**: the richest **10%** of people emit about half of CO2 while the poorest **50%** emit only ~10%; consumption-based CO2 per capita is high in only a few countries.
- **Addictive consumption** (John Ehrenfeld) - unrelated to real needs, harms health and social participation.
- **Overconsumption is not only about wealth**: everyday examples (AC, lights, food waste, single-use plastic, excess fertiliser) and North vs South differences.
- **Hyperconsumption** (Gilles Lipovetsky, 2011) - buying driven by novelty, speed and status, enabled by technology and easy credit.

nodes.label: Overconsumption
nodes.summary: Using resources more than needed or beyond the ecosystem's ability to recover, degrading environmental quality; a key driver of damage.
nodes.details:
**Overconsumption** is the **level of excessive consumption that drives environmental damage** - formally, **using resources more than needed or beyond the ecosystem's ability to recover, degrading environmental quality** (s30, s34; Heinrichs et al. 2016, *Sustainability Science*, ch. 5).

**Why people consume** - perspectives on consumption behaviour: **rational, cultural, pleasurable, identity, communication** (signalling status or progress).

**Overconsumption is not always about economic capability** (s33):
- **Global North**: consumptive lifestyles, high industrialisation.
- **Global South**: export of natural resources, rapid urbanisation. Lecturer's note: at macro level Southern overconsumption is hidden because only a small share of people overconsume - there is a big **gap between individuals**.

Overconsumption is the 'A' in IPAT made visible, the cause of **backfire** in the Jevons paradox, and what the **ecological footprint** measures. It reframes the population debate: **who consumes** matters more than **how many** people there are.
nodes.examTips: Define overconsumption and contrast it with hyperconsumption (need-exceeding vs status/novelty-driven). Argue 'overconsumption, not overpopulation' using footprint and CO2 data.

nodes.label: Consumption Inequality & CO2 Data
nodes.summary: Richest 10% emit roughly half of global CO2; poorest 50% only ~10%. Consumption-based CO2 per capita (2021) is high in few countries.
nodes.details:
Two pieces of evidence that **overconsumption is concentrated**:

1. **Emissions by income group** (s30, the widely cited Oxfam-style 'champagne glass' chart): when the world's population is ranked by income, the **richest 10%** account for a very large share of CO2 emissions (about half), while the **poorest 50%** - mostly in the Global South - account for **only ~10%**.
2. **CO2 emissions per capita based on consumption (2021) by country** (s31, map): emissions counted where goods are **consumed**, not produced. Dark (high) colours appear in **only a few places**; most of the world map is light, meaning **low consumption**.

Why consumption-based accounting matters: it assigns emissions from imported goods to the importing country, correcting for **offshoring** and making rich countries' true impact visible.

Lecturer's point: half of humanity contributes little to environmental damage; the problem lies with the overconsumption of a wealthy minority, mostly in the Global North.

nodes.label: Everyday Overconsumption & Planned Obsolescence
nodes.summary: AC set very cold all day, lights left on, oversized portions and food waste, single-use plastic, excess fertiliser; products built to fail.
nodes.details:
**Everyday examples of overconsumption** (s33):
- Using **air conditioning at very low temperatures all day**.
- **Turning on lights** when not in use.
- **Eating portions larger than needed** and leaving leftovers (food waste).
- **Single-use packaging** - plastic and disposable utensils.
- **Overusing fertilisers** beyond plants' needs (links to agricultural intensification trade-offs).

**Planned obsolescence** (lecturer's notes): products are designed with a **limited lifespan**, forcing repeat purchases:
- **Incandescent bulbs** limited to ~**1,000 hours** (the historic Phoebus cartel).
- **DuPont nylon stockings** - reportedly made less durable to sell more.
- **Electronics, furniture**, etc.

These show overconsumption is often habitual and built into products and systems, not just a matter of individual wealth - relevant to the discussion question on whether change can be individual or must be collective/policy-driven.

nodes.label: Addictive Consumption
nodes.summary: John Ehrenfeld: consumption that becomes addictive, unrelated to real needs, lowers individual health and social participation (e.g. obesity).
nodes.details:
**Overconsumption can become addictive** - consumption **not related to actual needs**.

- Concept from **John Ehrenfeld** (chemical engineer, sustainability thinker; *Sustainability by Design*).
- **Addictive consumption** results in **low levels of individual health** and **low participation in society** - people become self-focused.
- **Example: obesity** - overconsumption of food harming health.

Why it matters: it shows overconsumption harms not just the environment but **human wellbeing**, undermining the assumption that more consumption = a better life. It links to **hyperconsumption** (psychological/social drivers) and to the idea that sustainability requires redefining 'need' and 'enough'.

nodes.label: Hyperconsumption
nodes.summary: Lipovetsky (2011): buying driven by social/psychological factors (novelty, speed, status) far beyond functional need, with rapid turnover and duplication.
nodes.details:
**Hyperconsumption** (**Gilles Lipovetsky, 2011**): purchasing/using **driven by social and psychological factors far beyond functional needs** - **speed, novelty, status** - with **rapid turnover** and **many duplications**.

**Context**: geographical and time boundaries are increasingly **negligible** (anything can be bought anytime online); technology is **entrenched in daily life**; people want the **latest / most up-to-date** products.

**Drivers**: trends and technological advancement; easy credit - **loan modes such as PayLater, credit cards and instalment schemes** make buying easier.

**Overconsumption vs hyperconsumption**:
- *Overconsumption* = using **more than needed** or **beyond ecosystem recovery** -> environmental degradation.
- *Hyperconsumption* = buying for **novelty/identity**, far beyond function, with fast replacement.

Hyperconsumption is a powerful **A (affluence)** amplifier in IPAT and a main reason footprints of rich societies exceed biocapacity.
nodes.examTips: Most likely: 'Distinguish overconsumption from hyperconsumption with examples.' Name Lipovetsky (2011).

nodes.label: Hyperconsumption Examples
nodes.summary: Fast fashion, fast furniture, yearly gadget upgrades, duplicated skincare, frequent food delivery and buy-try-return e-commerce.
nodes.details:
Examples from the slide and lecturer's notes:

- **Fast fashion** - buying the latest styles **every month**; 'haul' clothes worn only **5-10 times**; wardrobe clear-outs each season.
- **Fast furniture** - cheap, **low-durability** furniture produced and discarded quickly.
- **Gadgets** - **replacing phones every year** for the newest model while the old one still works; owning several similar devices.
- **Cosmetics/skincare** - overlapping products, 10+ step routines with duplication.
- **Home decor** - seasonal themes, renting storage for rarely used items.
- **Food delivery** - ordering via apps several times a day for variety, generating lots of packaging waste.
- **E-commerce** - buy-try-return cycles as entertainment.

Common thread: **novelty and identity**, not function, plus **easy credit (PayLater, instalments)**. Each example multiplies resource use, waste and emissions - and many shift production impacts to other countries (fast fashion -> **unequal impact**).

nodes.label: Part 3.4: Ecological Footprint
nodes.summary: Ecological footprint measures human demand on nature in global hectares and compares it with biocapacity to reveal overshoot.
nodes.details:
Part 3.4 introduces a way to **measure** overconsumption against planetary limits.

- **Ecological footprint** - human demand for natural capital: land/sea area needed to provide resources and absorb waste.
- Compared with **biocapacity** - productive area available. Footprint > biocapacity = **ecological deficit / overshoot**. Globally we used **73% of biocapacity in 1961 vs 160% in 2020**.
- **Measured** in **global hectares (gha) per person per year** from food, housing energy/materials, mobility and waste.
- **Indonesia (2022)**: biocapacity 1.2 gha vs footprint 1.8 gha -> **deficit -0.6 gha**.
- **How many Earths**: USA ~5, India <1, world ~1.75.
- **Discussion**: calculate your own footprint and decide which changes are individual vs collective/policy.

nodes.label: Ecological Footprint: Concept
nodes.summary: A measure of human demand for natural capital: the biologically productive area needed to supply resources and absorb wastes.
nodes.details:
The **ecological footprint** is a **measure of human demand for natural capital** - the **amount of nature needed to support a person, population or economy**. In other words, a **measure of human impact on the environment**.

- Tracked via an **ecological accounting system** (Global Footprint Network) that measures the **land area required to provide resources for human activities and to absorb its waste** (e.g. forest area to absorb CO2).
- **The more resources an individual or society consumes, the larger its footprint.**
- Lecturer's plain version: *how much land do humans need to meet their needs and wants?*

Why it matters:
- It translates consumption into a single comparable unit (**global hectares**) and can be compared directly with **biocapacity**.
- It is the measurement tool for the **overconsumption** argument and the modern analogue of **carrying capacity** for humans.
- It connects to **planetary boundaries**: overshoot signals living outside the safe operating space.
nodes.examTips: Define ecological footprint precisely (demand for productive land/sea to supply resources AND absorb waste). Don't confuse with carbon footprint (only one component).

nodes.label: Footprint vs Biocapacity & Overshoot
nodes.summary: Footprint (area demanded) is compared with biocapacity (productive area available); humanity used 73% of biocapacity in 1961 and 160% in 2020.
nodes.details:
The calculation **compares**:
- **Ecological footprint** - the area of **biologically productive land needed** to supply everything humans consume (**demand**).
- **Biocapacity** - the area of **biologically productive land available** to produce what humans demand from nature (**supply**).

If **footprint > biocapacity**, there is an **ecological deficit** (nationally) or **overshoot** (globally): capacity has been exceeded and needs surpass what nature can regenerate.

**Global data** (Global Footprint Network, 'Busting our Biocapacity Budget'):
- **1961**: humanity used **73%** of Earth's biocapacity (within limits).
- **2020**: humanity used **160%** - roughly **1.6 Earths** - an overshoot also expressed as **Earth Overshoot Day**.

Connections: biocapacity is effectively **carrying capacity** in area units; overshoot is the footprint version of breaching **planetary boundaries**. Overshoot is possible only temporarily, by depleting stocks (forests, fish, groundwater) and accumulating waste (CO2).
nodes.examTips: Explain footprint vs biocapacity and what a deficit means. Quote 73% (1961) vs 160% (2020).

nodes.label: Measuring the Footprint (gha)
nodes.summary: Measured in global hectares (gha) per person per year from food, housing energy and materials, mobility, and waste.
nodes.details:
**Measurement at the individual level**:

- **Main unit: global hectare (gha) per person per year** - the average biologically productive land/sea area 'required' by our lifestyle. A global hectare is a hectare with world-average productivity, so different land types can be compared and summed.

**Components** measured:
1. **Food consumption** (diet, e.g. meat vs plant-based)
2. **Energy and material use for homes** (electricity, appliances, building)
3. **Mobility** (transportation and travel, e.g. car, flights)
4. **Waste produced**

The **Footprint Calculator** (footprintcalculator.org) estimates an individual's gha and how many Earths would be needed if everyone lived that way; the **Global Footprint Network data portal** gives national figures.

Why it matters: it lets individuals see which lifestyle choices dominate their impact and test reductions - the basis of the week's discussion task.
nodes.examTips: Know the unit (gha per person per year) and the four components.

nodes.label: Indonesia's Ecological Footprint (2022)
nodes.summary: Indonesia 2022: biocapacity 1.2 gha, footprint 1.8 gha per person: deficit of -0.6 gha; deficit since ~2000.
nodes.details:
**Indonesia (2022)** from the Global Footprint Network data portal:

- **Biocapacity per person: 1.2 gha**
- **Ecological footprint per person: 1.8 gha**
- **Biocapacity reserve/deficit: -0.6 gha** (a **deficit**)
- GDP per person ~**$4,788**; population ~**275.5 million**.

**Trend 1961-2024**: in **1961** Indonesia's biocapacity per person was high (~2.8 gha) and its footprint low (~1.5 gha) - a large **reserve**. Biocapacity per person declined steadily (population growth, land degradation) while the footprint slowly rose; the lines **crossed around 2000**, and Indonesia has run a **growing deficit** since then.

Interpretation: even a middle-income country with a modest per-capita footprint can overshoot when **population growth reduces biocapacity per person** and consumption rises - showing **P and A interact**. Students are encouraged to explore other countries on the website.

nodes.label: How Many Earths? Country Comparison
nodes.summary: If everyone lived like: USA ~5 Earths, Australia ~4.1-4.5, Germany 3.0, China ~2.2-2.4, India <1; world average ~1.7-1.75.
nodes.details:
**'How many Earths would be needed if the world's population lived like the residents of...'** (Global Footprint Network):

| Country | 2018 | 2022 |
|---|---|---|
| USA | 5.0 | 5.1 |
| Australia | 4.1 | 4.5 |
| South Korea | 3.5 | - |
| Russia | 3.3 | 3.4 |
| Germany | 3.0 | 3.0 |
| Japan | 2.8 | 2.9 |
| UK | 2.9 | 2.6 |
| China | 2.2 | 2.4 |
| Brazil | 1.8 | 1.6 |
| **India** | **0.7** | **0.8** |
| **World** | **1.7** | **1.75** |

**Lesson (lecturer's notes)**: **India has a far larger population than the USA**, yet its consumption can still be accommodated by **less than one Earth**, while the US lifestyle would require ~5. So it is **not only population that matters but how people consume** - the core 'overconsumption vs overpopulation' message of the week.
nodes.examTips: Use USA (~5 Earths) vs India (<1 Earth) to argue overconsumption matters more than overpopulation. World ~1.7 Earths.

nodes.label: Discussion: Reducing Your Footprint
nodes.summary: Calculate your footprint; what changes reduce it (consumption patterns, technology)? Which changes are individual vs collective or policy-based?
nodes.details:
**Discussion questions (s42)**:
1. Use the **Ecological Footprint calculator** (footprintcalculator.org). What result did you get?
2. What can you do to **change your footprint**? Link changes to reducing **excessive consumption** - via **consumption patterns** or with the help of **technology**.
3. **Can all changes be made individually?** Which can be done at the individual level, and which must be **collective**, or through **government or global policy**?

**Model answer outline**:
- *Individual*: eat less meat and waste less food; use public transport, cycle or walk; fly less; save electricity (AC, lights); buy less and repair/reuse (avoid fast fashion and yearly gadget upgrades); avoid single-use plastic.
- *Technology-aided*: rooftop solar, efficient appliances, EVs - while watching for **Jevons rebound**.
- *Collective/policy*: public transport and cycling infrastructure, renewable grids, carbon pricing, bans on single-use plastic, right-to-repair and anti-obsolescence rules, building codes, international agreements.
- Many footprint components (grid electricity mix, urban form, product design) are **structural**, so individual action is necessary but **not sufficient**.
